extracted.intended_audience: Attorneys and registered patent practitioners who practice before the United States Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO); Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED); counsel to practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Rules, duties, and procedural standards governing ethical practice and discipline for practitioners before the USPTO, with examples of prohibited conduct (conflicts, communication failures, inventorship lapses) and the sanctions/remedies imposed in an agreed settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.107 — conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Representing a client when the representation of one client will be directly adverse to another client; representing a client when the representation of that client may be materially limited by the practitioner's responsibilities to another client; representing a client when the representation involves the assertion of the claim by one client against another client represented by the practitioner in the same proceeding without obtaining consent after full disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied to joint representation situations: the practitioner must identify and disclose actual or potential conflicts and obtain informed consent after full disclosure before continuing representation. Anti-patterns illustrated: undertaking joint representation of multiple applicants, continuing to represent both after an inventorship dispute, and naming one party as sole inventor without informed consent from the other.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(1)-(5) and (b) — communication and informed consent duties
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) A practitioner shall: (1) Promptly inform the client of any decision or circumstance with respect to which the client's informed consent is required; (2) Reasonably consult with the client about the means by which the client's objectives are to be accomplished; (3) Keep the client reasonably informed about the status of the matter; (4) Promptly comply with reasonable requests for information from the client; and (5) Consult with the client about any relevant limitation on the practitioner's conduct when the practitioner knows that the client expects assistance not permitted by the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct or other law. (b) A practitioner shall explain a matter to the extent reasonably necessary to permit the client to make informed decisions regarding the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical expectations: promptly notify clients of decisions requiring consent, consult on strategy and means, provide status updates, promptly respond to information requests, and explain limitations. Anti-patterns: failing to tell a co-client they were excluded as an inventor; giving inconsistent statements about inventorship; not explaining the practitioner’s role and scope of representation. Failure to satisfy these duties may be basis for discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to identify client(s), explain role, and define scope of representation before filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent 'failed to properly explain his role, identify his client(s), and identify the scope of his representation as to each client ... prior to filing the [provisional] application.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Best practice: before undertaking work (e.g., filing provisional or nonprovisional applications), clarify in writing who the client(s) are, the practitioner's role for each, and the scope of services. Lack of such clarity increases risk of conflicts and discipline. Use engagement agreements and conflict-checking procedures to prevent this failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to advise of potential conflicts and obtain informed consent before related representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent 'did not advise either Mr. Holland or Dr. McNaughton of any potential conflicts of interest and did not obtain informed consent from either client prior to undertaking the trademark representation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representations overlap (e.g., patent and related trademark work for parties with intertwined interests), practitioners must disclose potential conflicts and secure informed consent from each affected client before proceeding. Failure to do so (especially when one client later becomes adverse) violates conflict rules and can lead to withdrawal and discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to conduct an independent inventorship analysis prior to signing/filing patent applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent 'failed to conduct an independent analysis to determine the inventive entity prior to signing and filing either the provisional or the nonprovisional patent applications.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners must independently determine and verify the correct inventive entity (who qualifies as inventor/co-inventor) before executing filings that assert inventorship. Anti-patterns: relying solely on one client's statements, failing to inquire when disputes arise, and filing applications listing an incorrect sole inventor without informing others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to communicate inventorship status and changes to co-inventors
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent did not inform Dr. McNaughton that he was not named as a co-inventor on the nonprovisional application and gave conflicting statements about entitlement to inventorship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should promptly inform individuals of decisions affecting inventorship, provide relevant documents (e.g., claims), obtain necessary signatures/assignments, and advise on alternatives. Conflicting explanations or withholding information about inventorship status violate communication/informed consent obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of written engagement/representation agreements to clarify relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Fact noted: 'Respondent did not enter into a written engagement agreement with clients, Mr. Scott Holland and Dr. James McNaughton.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although the Order does not cite a specific regulation requiring a written agreement, the document implies that written engagement agreements help clarify client identity, scope, fee arrangements, and conflicts; practitioners are expected to use written agreements as a preventive measure against disputes and ethical lapses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating and aggravating factors considered in discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors reflected in the agreed upon resolution include: (i) Respondent has no prior disciplinary history before the USPTO; and (ii) Respondent fully cooperated with the OED during the investigation and resolution of this matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cooperation with disciplinary investigations and absence of prior misconduct may mitigate sanctions; conversely, recurrence of similar misconduct or failure to cooperate may be aggravating. The Office may consider these factors when determining appropriate discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions, remediation, reporting, and publication requirements available/ordered in settlement
rubrics_metrics.description: Agreed sanctions in this Final Order include: public reprimand; attendance in person of two ethics CLE classes pertaining to conflicts of interest within one year; reporting CLE attendance to the OED Director; taking and passing the MPRE with a grade of at least 85 and reporting the grade within one year; OED Director compliance with 37 C.F.R. § 11.59; electronic publication of the Final Order in the OED Reading Room; and publication of a Notice of Reprimand in the Official Gazette.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions can combine public discipline, mandatory education, examination requirements, reporting obligations, and public disclosure. Practitioners should expect publication of disciplinary outcomes and that imposed remedial steps must be completed within specified timeframes. The Office can also consider the record in future disciplinary proceedings (as aggravation or rebuttal).

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO jurisdiction and statutory/regulatory basis for disciplinary proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director has jurisdiction pursuant to 35 U.S.C. §§ 2(b)(2)(D) and 32 and 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.19 and 11.26; practitioners registered to practice before the USPTO are subject to the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners registered before the USPTO must comply with federal statutes and USPTO regulations governing professional conduct. Disciplinary processes are governed by those statutory and regulatory provisions; parties may enter settlement agreements resolving disciplinary action subject to Director approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Office may consider past disciplinary record in future matters (use as aggravating factor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nothing in the Agreement or Final Order prevents the Office from considering the record of this disciplinary proceeding when addressing any further complaint or evidence of the same or similar misconduct concerning Respondent; in any future disciplinary proceeding the record may be considered as an aggravating factor and/or to rebut statements by Respondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practitioners should understand that prior settlements/orders can be cited in future disciplinary proceedings to justify harsher sanctions or to rebut mitigation claims. Maintaining compliance and corrective steps is important to minimize future exposure.
